content: Testing and conducting exercises to evaluate community mitigation interventions are essential because most communities have not experienced disasters on the scale of a severe pandemic. Drills and exercises are critical to assess the effectiveness of preparedness plans. A severe pandemic would challenge all aspects of governmental and community functions. Therefore, advanced planning is necessary to ensure a coordinated communication strategy and the continuity of essential services. Realistic exercises that account for the effects of proposed interventions and their cascading secondand third-order consequences will help identify gaps in planning and resource allocation. It is acknowledged that additional research is required to validate the proposed interventions, assess their effectiveness, and identify any adverse consequences. This research will be conducted as soon as feasible and will inform updated guidance as needed. A proposed research agenda is outlined within this document. Planning and preparing for the implementation of mitigation strategies during a pandemic are complex tasks that require the involvement of all levels of government and all segments of society. Community-level intervention strategies will necessitate specific actions by individuals, families, employers, schools, and other organizations. Building a foundation of community, individual, and family preparedness, as well as developing and delivering effective risk communication to the public in advance of a pandemic, is critical. If these efforts are embraced earnestly, they will enhance the ability to respond not only to pandemic influenza but also to a variety of other hazards and threats. While the challenge is formidable, the consequences of facing a severe pandemic unprepared would be intolerable. This interim pre-pandemic planning guidance is presented as a step in our commitment to addressing the challenge of mitigating a pandemic by building and enhancing community resilience. A severe pandemic in a fully susceptible population, such as the 1918 pandemic or one of even greater severity, with limited quantities of antiviral medications and pre-pandemic vaccines, represents a worst-case scenario for pandemic planning and preparedness. However, because pandemics are unpredictable in terms of timing, onset, and severity, communities must plan and prepare for the full spectrum of pandemic severity that could occur. The purpose of this document is to provide interim planning guidance for what are currently believed to be the most effective combinations of pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) for mitigating the impact of an influenza pandemic across a wide range of severity scenarios. The community strategy for pandemic influenza mitigation supports the goals of the Federal Government's response to pandemic influenza: to limit the spread of a pandemic, mitigate disease, suffering, and death, sustain infrastructure, and lessen the impact on the economy and societal functioning. In a pandemic, the overarching public health imperative must be to reduce morbidity and mortality. From a public health perspective, failure to protect human health is likely to result in failure to achieve the goals of preserving societal function and mitigating the social and economic consequences of a severe pandemic. Inventories of physical assets, such as emergency services capacity, inpatient beds, ICU beds, and ventilators, as well as the numbers of healthcare professionals, including nurses and physicians, are critical. The most prudent approach, therefore, appears to be expanding medical surge capacity as much as possible while simultaneously reducing the anticipated demand for services by limiting disease transmission. Delaying a rapid upswing of cases and lowering the epidemic peak to the extent possible would allow for a better match between the number of ill individuals requiring hospitalization and the nation's capacity to provide medical care for such individuals. The primary strategies for combating influenza include: 1) Vaccination, 2) Treatment of infected individuals and prophylaxis of exposed individuals with influenza antiviral medications, and 3) Implementation of infection control and social distancing measures. Vaccination will be the single most effective intervention. However, it is highly unlikely that a well-matched vaccine will be available at the onset of a pandemic unless a vaccine with broad cross-protection is developed. With current vaccine technology, a pandemic strain vaccine would not become available for at least 4 to 6 months after the start of a pandemic, although this lag time may be reduced in the future. Furthermore, once an effective pandemic vaccine is developed and being produced, it is likely that the quantities will be limited due to the production process and will not be sufficient to cover the entire population. Pre-pandemic vaccines may be available at the onset of a pandemic, but there is no guarantee that they will be effective against the emerging pandemic strain.
